title: ABSALOM SLEPT WITH DAVID’S CONCUBINES: WHY HE DID IT WHERE ISRAEL COULD KNOW
paragraphs: ABSALOM SLEPT WITH DAVID’S CONCUBINES: WHY HE DID IT WHERE ISRAEL COULD KNOW

It was not merely sexual sin. It was rebellion turned into a public declaration—and behind that rooftop scandal stood an earlier secret sin, a wounded kingdom, a devastating word of judgment, and a warning that still reaches into the hidden rooms of our lives.
There are passages in the Bible we read slowly because they comfort us.
And then there are passages we read slowly because we almost cannot believe they are there.
This is one of them.
David—the shepherd boy who faced Goliath, the psalmist who sang to God in caves, the king through whose family line the Messiah would come—is fleeing Jerusalem.
Not from the Philistines.
Not from Saul.
Not from a foreign army.
From his own son.
Absalom.

The handsome prince who had stolen the hearts of Israel has declared himself king. David has abandoned Jerusalem, crossing the Kidron and moving toward the wilderness while his kingdom fractures behind him.
But Absalom does not merely want David's throne.
Something happens on a rooftop in Jerusalem that turns political rebellion into something far more personal, humiliating, and horrifying.
David had left ten concubines behind to care for the royal house when he fled Jerusalem.
Then Absalom asked Ahithophel, his counselor, what he should do next.
Ahithophel gave him advice that sounds almost unbelievable:
“Go in unto thy father's concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father.”
Then Scripture records the result:
“So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.”
—2 Samuel 16:21–22, KJV
Do not rush past those final words.
“In the sight of all Israel.”
The Hebrew is:
לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל
leʿênei kol-Yisra'el
Literally, the expression carries the sense of “before the eyes of all Israel” or “in the sight of all Israel.”
That phrase is the doorway into understanding the horror of this scene.

The text does not require us to imagine that the sexual acts themselves were physically performed in open view before a watching crowd. Scripture says a tent was pitched for Absalom on the roof. The point is that what he was doing was made publicly known. The rooftop setting transformed the act into a visible political declaration.
Everyone was supposed to understand what Absalom had done.
That was precisely the strategy.
Ahithophel tells him that “all Israel shall hear.”
This was calculated.

Absalom was being urged to cross a line so publicly and offensively that reconciliation with David would appear impossible. His followers would therefore have less reason to fear that father and son might eventually reconcile and leave the rebels exposed.
In other words, Ahithophel was telling Absalom:
Burn the bridge.
Make the rebellion irreversible.
Show Israel that you have completely rejected your father.
And Absalom did it.
But there is another layer.
A terrifying one.
Because years earlier, another man had committed sexual sin.
Not Absalom.
David.
And David had tried to keep it hidden.
David saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah.
He took her.
She became pregnant.
David attempted to manipulate circumstances so Uriah would believe the child was his.
When that failed, David arranged for Uriah to be placed where the fighting was fiercest and then abandoned in battle.
Uriah died.
David took Bathsheba as his wife.
From the outside, perhaps the scandal appeared buried.
But heaven had seen everything.
God sent Nathan the prophet.
And after Nathan exposed David's sin, he delivered words that must have echoed through David's memory years later when news came from Jerusalem.
God declared:
“I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house.”
Then came the chilling words:
“I will take thy wives before thine eyes, and give them unto thy neighbour, and he shall lie with thy wives in the sight of this sun.”
And then:
“For thou didst it secretly: but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.”
—2 Samuel 12:11–12, KJV
Read that again.
Secretly.
Before all Israel.
David sinned behind closed doors.
Years later, judgment erupted from within his own household and became publicly visible.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 12:12 makes the contrast especially sharp:
כִּי אַתָּה עָשִׂיתָ בַסָּתֶר
ki attah asita basater
“For you did it in secret.”
But what follows would happen:
נֶגֶד כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל וְנֶגֶד הַשָּׁמֶשׁ
neged kol-Yisra'el weneged hashamesh
“before all Israel and before the sun.”
Hidden sin.
Public consequences.
And suddenly the rooftop in 2 Samuel 16 becomes even more disturbing.
Because Absalom did not merely choose a sexually immoral act.
The biblical narrative connects this episode with Nathan's earlier prophecy.
David's secret sin had not disappeared simply because time had passed.
This does not mean Absalom was innocent.
It does not mean God forced Absalom to sin.
Scripture consistently treats human beings as morally responsible for their actions. Absalom willingly rebelled. Ahithophel deliberately counseled him. The wickedness belonged to those committing it.
Yet God had already announced that consequences would rise from David's own house.
That distinction matters.
God's sovereignty over history never transforms evil into righteousness.
And God's judgment on David never makes the women involved disposable characters.
They were real women caught inside the catastrophe created by powerful men.
David had left ten concubines behind to care for the palace. Absalom then used them as instruments in his rebellion against his father.

Later, after David returned to Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 20:3 records another painful detail: David provided for these women but no longer had relations with them, and they lived in confinement, described as living in widowhood until their deaths.
The scandal had consequences far beyond the men whose names dominate the story.
That matters because sin almost never stays inside the boundaries the sinner imagines.
Someone else eventually bleeds.
Someone else carries memories they never asked for.
Someone else lives inside consequences created by decisions they never made.
And perhaps that is where this ancient rooftop suddenly becomes uncomfortable.
Because you may not be David.
You may not be Absalom.
You may never sit on a throne.
But you know what a locked door feels like.
You know what it means to have something you desperately hope nobody discovers.
The private browser history.
The secret conversation.
The emotional affair you keep calling “just friendship.”
The bitterness you feed when nobody is around.
The addiction hidden behind respectable Christianity.
The money nobody knows about.
The lie your spouse believes.
The resentment beneath your worship.
The pornography followed by prayer.
The secret messages deleted before anyone can see them.
The compromise you have repeatedly promised God would be “the last time.”
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your family does not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe the people who admire your faith would never suspect it.
But David's story whispers something frightening across thousands of years:
Hidden does not mean healed.
And secret does not mean safe.
David learned that.
But we must also say something equally important.
David's story is not teaching that every suffering person is being publicly punished for some secret sin.
That would be cruel theology, and Scripture does not permit us to make that assumption.
Job suffered without the secret wickedness his friends imagined.
Jesus rejected the simplistic idea that particular suffering automatically proves particular personal sin.
So do not read someone else's tragedy and appoint yourself God's detective.
Read David's story first as a mirror.
Not a weapon.
Ask what you are hiding.
Because there is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says:
Come into the light.
Condemnation says:
Stay in the darkness because God could never want you now.
And that second voice is a liar.
David's sin was horrific.
Adultery.
Deception.
Abuse of royal power.
Bloodshed.
There is no reason to soften it.
Nathan did not soften it.
God did not call evil good.
But when Nathan confronted David, David finally stopped hiding.
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
—2 Samuel 12:13
No royal speech.
No public-relations campaign.
No blaming Bathsheba.
No blaming stress.
No blaming loneliness.
No blaming the pressures of kingship.
“I have sinned.”
And Nathan answered:
“The LORD also hath put away thy sin.”
Grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not consequence-free grace.
David would still experience devastating consequences.
His family would fracture.
Violence would enter his house.
Absalom would rebel.
The king would weep.
But forgiveness had entered the story.
This is where Christianity becomes radically different from simply telling people to become better.
The Gospel does not say:
Hide your scandal more effectively.
The Gospel says:
Bring your scandal to the Savior.
Because centuries after David fled Jerusalem because of a rebellious son, another Son of David would approach Jerusalem.
Jesus Christ.
David crossed the Kidron in grief.
Jesus would cross the Kidron on the way toward Gethsemane.
David suffered partly amid consequences connected to his own sin.
Jesus had no sin of His own.
David needed forgiveness.
Jesus came to provide it.
David could write songs about mercy.
Jesus would purchase mercy with His blood.
And on another public hill outside Jerusalem, shame would once again be displayed before watching eyes.
But this time the Man being humiliated was innocent.
Jesus was stripped.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Crucified.
The sinless Son of God bore shame He did not deserve so guilty people could receive grace they could never earn.
That is the Gospel.
Not that your sin doesn't matter.
It mattered enough for Christ to die.
Not that judgment isn't real.
The cross proves how serious sin is.
Not that repentance is optional.
Jesus called sinners to repent.
But the cross also announces something breathtaking:
Your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
David's story contains adultery, murder, family collapse, rebellion, humiliation, grief, and consequences that cannot simply be erased.
Yet Scripture does not end with Absalom standing on David's rooftop.
The promises of God keep moving.
Generation after generation.
Until Matthew opens the New Testament:
“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David…”
Do you see it?
David's scandal could not cancel God's redemptive purpose.
That does not excuse David.
It magnifies grace.
And maybe somebody reading this has spent years believing the thing you did disqualified you forever.
Maybe you have repented, but you still introduce yourself internally by your worst moment.
Adulterer.
Addict.
Liar.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Unclean.
Ruined.
Maybe nobody calls you those things anymore.
But you do.
Every morning.
Every night.
Every time you try to pray.
Listen carefully.
Repentance does not mean pretending the past never happened.
Grace does not rewrite history by calling evil good.
Jesus does something greater.
He redeems sinners.
He takes people who cannot repair themselves and gives them something they could never manufacture:
forgiveness.
A new heart.
A new identity.
A new direction.
A new life.
That is why the message is not “David was actually a good man who made a tiny mistake.”
No.
David sinned grievously.
The message is that David's God is astonishingly merciful to repentant sinners.
And that same mercy has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe your rooftop has not happened.
Maybe what is secret is still secret.
Then do not wait for destruction to teach you what conviction is already telling you.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Cut off what feeds the sin.
Tell the truth where truth must be told.
Seek wise biblical help.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Stop calling bondage “a struggle” when you have secretly decided to protect it.
Stop asking Jesus to comfort the version of you that refuses to surrender.
Grace is not God's permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
Walk out.
And if consequences remain after repentance, do not mistake consequences for abandonment.
David was forgiven before every consequence disappeared.
Sometimes God removes guilt while allowing consequences to become teachers.
Sometimes healing takes years.
Sometimes trust must be rebuilt slowly.
Sometimes what was broken cannot be restored exactly as it was.
But forgiven people can still walk with God through consequences.
That is grace too.
Maybe you are not David in this story.
Maybe you feel more like someone standing beneath the rooftop.
Someone else's choices wounded you.
Someone else's selfishness changed your life.
Someone else's secret became your trauma.
Someone else's rebellion left scars on your body, your family, your trust, or your faith.
Hear this too:
You are not merely collateral damage in somebody else's story.
Jesus sees you.
The women in 2 Samuel 16 remind us never to preach about the failures of powerful men while forgetting those who suffered because of them.
Christ sees the overlooked.
He sees those who were used.
He sees those who were betrayed.
He sees those who survived what somebody else decided.
And His grace is not only for the guilty person seeking forgiveness.
His presence is also for the wounded person seeking healing.
This is why the Gospel is bigger than scandal.
Scandal says, “Look what happened.”
Grace says, “Look what Christ can redeem.”
Scandal exposes.
Grace transforms.
Scandal can become the chapter everyone remembers.
But Jesus Christ still holds the pen over the surrendered life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not write a polished Christian answer just to impress strangers.
Be honest.
And if Christ has already carried you through a chapter you once thought would destroy you, tell someone below. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needs tonight.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
Because some truths need to be reread when temptation starts negotiating with you again.

Someone scrolling tonight may be hiding something that is slowly destroying them. Someone may believe their scandal has placed them beyond Christ's mercy. Someone may desperately need to discover that repentance is still possible, forgiveness is still real, and Jesus still receives sinners.
We do not buy grace.
We do not purchase God's blessing.
Christ has already paid the price sinners could never pay.

But if you want to glorify God by helping biblical truth reach more people, one practical way you can participate is by supporting Gospel-centered work, sharing these messages publicly, and helping us continue creating resources that point people toward Jesus.
You never know who is hiding behind a smile.
You never know who has convinced themselves that God could never forgive what they have done.
You never know whose secret war may be interrupted because you were willing to put the Gospel in front of them.
Absalom's tent stood on a rooftop where Israel could know what had happened.
David's hidden sin eventually came into the light.
But neither David's secret nor Absalom's scandal gets the final word in the biblical story.
Jesus does.
So bring Him the chapter you wish you could tear out.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the consequences.
Bring Him the wound somebody else gave you.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the heart you cannot repair.
Repent where you have sinned.
Receive grace where Christ offers forgiveness.
Seek healing where you have been wounded.
And stop believing that darkness gets to write the ending.
Because the most unforgettable thing about your scandal may one day be the grace of Christ that met you there.
